CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Engage constructively at the G20 Osaka meeting with Trump this weekend, seeking a tariff ceasefire and restart of negotiations. Do not make major structural concessions but signal willingness to increase purchases and discuss IP protections. Avoid escalation — the economy is too fragile and Huawei is too exposed to risk a further spiral. Use the G20 window to buy time.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is elevated but not existential. Three factors drive the +0.55 reading. First, the Huawei Entity List designation (May 16) is a direct strike at China's tech champion — Google has suspended Android access, US chip suppliers have paused sales, and the 90-day temporary license expires August 19 (timeline entry 2019-05-16, 2019-05-20). This threatens Made in China 2025 ambitions and 5G leadership. Second, Trump has threatened 25% tariffs on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese exports (timeline entry 2019-05-05), which would cover consumer electronics and directly hit Chinese manufacturers. Third, economic data is weakening — April retail sales fell to 7.2% (16-year low) and industrial production dropped to 5.4% vs 6.5% expected (CNBC, 2019-05-15), casting doubt on the Q1 recovery. The IMF cut its 2019 growth forecast to 6.2% citing trade tensions (Reuters, 2019-06-05).

However, China is not cornered. Beijing has room for stimulus — six RRR cuts since 2018, fast-tracked infrastructure spending, and tax cuts worth trillions of yuan (Reuters, 2019-06-05). The IMF says current stimulus is sufficient to stabilize growth absent further escalation. China retains leverage through rare earths (Xi's May 20 factory visit was a clear signal), the unreliable entity list announcement (May 31), and its role as the US's second-largest creditor. The rare earth threat, while likely bluster in practice (Business Insider, 2019-06-02), has already prompted the Pentagon to seek new funding for domestic production — showing it has deterrent value even without execution.

The action recommendation is negotiate at slight firmness (-0.1) because: (a) the G20 is a natural venue with low expectations — any positive signal moves markets favorably; (b) escalation would be self-defeating — triggering the $300B tariff tranche and deeper Huawei restrictions would compound the economic slowdown; (c) Trump faces his own pressures (US GDP growth averaging 2.4%, election cycle approaching, farm-belt frustration) and may be open to a deal that lets him claim victory; (d) but China should not concede on structural issues (industrial policy, sovereignty) without matching US concessions on Huawei and tariffs. The optimal play is a G20 truce that halts further escalation and reopens talks.
key_factors: Huawei Entity List (May 16) threatens tech supply chain and 5G ambitions
Threatened $300B tariff tranche would hit consumer goods directly
Weakening economic data: retail sales at 16-year low, IP miss in April
IMF cut 2019 GDP forecast to 6.2% on trade tensions
Rare earth leverage provides counter-deterrent but experts doubt execution
G20 Osaka meeting imminent — natural de-escalation window
China has fiscal/monetary stimulus room to absorb short-term tariff impact
US also faces costs: tariff pass-through to consumers, 0.5% annual GDP drag

sources_cited.excerpt: US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Same day: Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi.

Trump tweets that negotiations are going 'too slowly' and that China is attempting to 'renegotiate.' Orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and directs preparation of tariffs on remaining Chinese imports (~$300B).
China announces it will establish an 'unreliable entity list' targeting foreign firms that cut supplies to Chinese companies for non-commercial reasons.
Trump and Xi agree by phone to meet at the G20 in Osaka.
China's retail sales rose 7.2% in April, the slowest pace in 16 years. China's April industrial production rose 5.4%, less than the 6.5% expected or the 8.5% gain in March.
The International Monetary Fund cut its 2019 economic growth forecast for China to 6.2% on heightened uncertainty around trade frictions.
If Trump went ahead and tariffed a combined $500 billion of Chinese imports, it would be the equivalent of roughly 4% of China's GDP.
Rare-earth experts believe Beijing won't follow through with rare earth threats, with one expert calling them just 'loud saber-rattling' to get Washington back to the negotiating table.
The White House has downplayed expectations of a deal. The likeliest course is a temporary truce that leaves existing tariffs in place, but postpones additional taxes on Chinese imports.
